P.1 Extended modules and cross-level structures
The ontology of continua is organised as a hierarchical sequence of levels
K0 , K1 , . . . , K12 ,
each representing a qualitatively distinct form of structure, dynamics, and admissible states. Every level
Kx possesses:
• a state space Ω(Kx ),
• a set of axes A(Kx ),
• potentials P (Kx ),
• thresholds Θ(Kx ),
• flows J(Kx ),
• cycles C(Kx ) with characteristic times τ (Kx ),
• a continuum measure k(Kx ),
• and a boundary ∂Ω(Kx ) describing the conditions of collapse or transition.
Each Kx is embedded into a corresponding meta-space Mx that determines the admissible axes and
states:
A(Kx ) ⊆ A(Mx ),
Ω(Kx ) ⊆ Ω(Mx ).
The meta-space restricts the degrees of freedom available to the continuum and thereby shapes its evolution.
P.1.1 Dimensional Growth and Transitions Kx → Kx+1
A transition from level Kx to Kx+1 occurs when:
1. a new class of differences emerges that cannot be represented within the existing axes A(Kx );
2. structural tension exceeds a threshold:
T (Kx ) > Θdim (Kx );
3. the meta-space requires a higher-dimensional representation;
4. the existing configuration space Ω(Kx ) becomes insuﬀicient or collapses onto its boundary
∂Ω(Kx ).
This process is irreversible:
dim Kx+1 ≥ dim Kx ,
and any “reduction” of dimensionality corresponds to the death of the continuum:
Ω(Kx ) = ∅.

188

P.1.2 Universal Structure Across All Levels
Despite the qualitative diversity of levels, every Kx shares a common formal structure. The evolution of
a continuum is governed by:

Kx (t + dt) = E Kx (t), Mx (t) ,
where E is an evolution operator constrained by the meta-space Mx . A continuum evolves only within
the admissible region of its meta-space:
Kx (t + dt) ∈ Ω(Mx )

or the evolution is forbidden.

The continuum measure is:
k(Kx ) = kΩ · kA · kC · kJ · kT ,
where:
• kΩ measures the volume of allowed states,
• kA counts realised axes relative to the meta-space,
• kC reflects stability of cycles,
• kJ describes coherence of flows,
• kT measures structural tension relative to thresholds.
P.1.3 Hierarchy of Levels K0 → K12
Each level represents a distinct stratum of organisation:
• K0 — meta-pressure, possibility conditions, and pre-structural logic;
• K1 — continuous one-dimensional continua;
• K2 — two-dimensional continua with internal flows and clusters;
• K3 — chemical configuration spaces and reaction manifolds;
• K4 — protocell-level continua with membranes and boundaries;
• K5 — neural continua with excitation cycles and attractors;
• K6 — cognitive continua with predictive models;
• K7 — social continua with group-level stability cycles;
• K8 — civilisational continua with large-scale coordination flows;
• K9 — theoretical continua (structure of explanations);
• K10 — meta-theoretical continua (structure of structural spaces);
• K11 — formal ontologies and logic-level continua;
• K12 — meta-ontological continua governing the possibility space of all lower levels.
Higher levels do not replace lower ones; they embed and extend them:
K x ⊆ Mx ,

Mx ⊆ Ω(Kx+1 ).

189

P.1.4 Boundaries, Collapse and Death of Continua
Every Kx has a boundary ∂Ω(Kx ) where the continuum loses admissibility. A continuum dies when:
Ω(Kx ) = ∅

⇒

k(Kx ) = 0,

which corresponds to:
• violation of thresholds Θ(Kx ),
• loss of stable cycles C(Kx ),
• destructive flows reaching critical values,
• collapse of axes or incompatibility with Mx .
Death is distinct from evolution: it removes the continuum from the space of admissible structures
and cannot be undone.
P.1.5 Role of k-Level Structure in the Core Model
The K-levels provide the vertical backbone of the Ontology of Continua. They:
• organise emergence from physical to cognitive to social to meta-ontological structures;
• define the recursion Kx → Mx → Kx+1 ;
• supply the dimensional ladder necessary for universal applicability;
• constrain the evolution of continua via admissibility conditions;
• unify all domains of reality under one mathematical framework.
The structure of K-levels makes the ontology both hierarchical and recursive: every level depends on
the meta-space above it and constrains the level below.
P.1.6 K0 Overview
Level K0 represents the pre-structural foundation of all continua. It is not a physical or geometric domain
but the logical substrate that defines the conditions of possibility for any continuum Kx . It provides
the metapressure, admissibility constraints, logical superiority (Axiom 0.3), and the universal rules that
govern which structures may exist.
K0 does not itself possess the conventional axes or geometric dimensions. Instead, it specifies:
• the meta-laws L determining structural coherence,
• the possibility space P for all continua,
• the metapressure driving emergence of differences,
• the universal thresholds that define admissibility and collapse,
• the recursion rules Kx 7→ Mx 7→ Kx+1 .
Its primary function is logical governance of all deeper levels.
P.1.7 State Space Ω(K0 )
Ω(K0 ) consists of all admissible configurations of the pair
(P, L),
where P is the meta-domain of possible structures and L is the system of meta-laws that enforce coherence.
Because K0 is pre-geometric, Ω(K0 ) is not a metric space but an abstract set with the following
properties:
190

1. Ω(K0 ) contains all possible specifications of structural constraints that allow continua to exist.
2. Ω(K0 ) has no internal topology unless induced by constraints in L.
3. Every Ω(Kx ) for x ≥ 1 is a subset of Ω(K0 ):
Ω(Kx ) ⊆ Ω(K0 ).
There is no continuous evolution inside Ω(K0 ); it defines conditions, not dynamical trajectories.
P.1.8 Boundary ∂Ω(K0 )
The boundary of K0 consists of all meta-configurations that violate internal coherence conditions of the
meta-laws L.
A configuration (P, L) lies on ∂Ω(K0 ) if:
• the laws contradict each other,
• admissibility collapses (P becomes empty),
• recursion rules become undefined,
• structural consistency conditions cannot be maintained.
Crossing ∂Ω(K0 ) corresponds to the logical impossibility of any continuum.
P.1.9 Axes A(K0 )
K0 has no geometric axes. Instead it contains:
• abstract axes of possibility,
• admissibility axes governing which structures can be produced,
• meta-axes that define the logical dependencies among levels.
In formal terms:
A(K0 ) = {dimensions of admissible structural variation}.
These are the ultimate sources of all later axes:
A(Kx ) ⊆ A(K0 ).
P.1.10 Potentials P (K0 )
Potentials at K0 describe meta-conditions that push continua toward structure:
P (K0 ) = {pressures, constraints, logical gradients}.
They include:
• metapressure (Axiom 0.z),
• pressure toward structuralisation,
• pressure toward compatible differences,
• pressure toward nonempty admissible spaces.
These potentials are not numeric energies but logical intensities.

191

P.1.11 Thresholds Θ(K0 )
Thresholds at K0 correspond to logical break-points:
Θ(K0 ) = {Θcoh , Θadm , Θmeta }.
Examples:
• Θcoh : minimal coherence of meta-laws,
• Θadm : minimal non-empty possibility space,
• Θmeta : minimal support for recursion.
If any threshold is violated, no continuum can exist at any Kx .
P.1.12 Flows J(K0 )
There are no physical flows at K0 . J(K0 ) instead contains:
• flows of admissibility,
• flows of logical dependence,
• propagation of constraints,
• meta-flows describing which structures can generate others.
These flows shape the space of possible continua but do not correspond to time evolution.
P.1.13 Cycles C(K0 )
Cycles at K0 correspond to:
• fixed-point consistency cycles,
• meta-stability loops of admissibility,
• self-referential closure cycles in L.
A cycle exists if:
Π(C) > Θcoh ,
where Π(C) is the “power” of the meta-cycle (stability of recursive closure).
There are no temporal cycles; these are purely logical cycles.
P.1.14 Time τ (K0 )
Time does not exist at K0 .
Theorem “Emergence of Time from C-cycles” (Physics Run):
Time emerges when Ω(K2 ) contains a non-degradable cycle C with:
Π(C) > Θtime .
Thus:
τ (K0 ) undefined.

192

P.1.15 Continuumness k(K0 )
Continuumness measures the admissibility of all continua:
k(K0 ) = H(Ω(K0 )) · kA (K0 ) · kcoh (K0 ),
where:
• H(Ω(K0 )) = 1 if Ω(K0 ) 6= ∅, else 0,
• kA (K0 ) measures the richness of admissible axes,
• kcoh measures meta-law coherence.
If k(K0 ) = 0, no continuum at any higher level can exist.
P.1.16 Structural Tension T (K0 )
Structural tension is:
T (K0 ) = T (P, L),
representing the degree of incompatibility within meta-laws or between meta-laws and admissible structures.
High tension may:
• reduce admissible sets,
• produce incompatible branches,
• collapse Ω(K0 ).
P.1.17 Energy E(K0 )
There is no physical energy at K0 . Instead:
E(K0 ) = Emeta ,
a formal measure of internal support for consistent structures:
Emeta ∝ coherence of L.
P.1.18 Operators on K0 (Ψ, Φ, Λ, U , X)
Operators at K0 govern admissibility and recursion:
• Ψ: operator of level creation
Ψ : Kx 7→ Mx+1
• Φ: operator of meta-space evolution
Φ : Mx 7→ Mx (t + dt)
• Λ: constraint operator enforcing L
• U : operator of structural unification
• X: operator of logical branching (Axiom 21)
These operators define the backbone of vertical recursion.

193

P.1.19 Processes on K0
Key processes:
• logical unification,
• admissibility expansion/contraction,
• meta-stabilisation of recursive definitions,
• branching of possibility spaces,
• collapse of incompatible meta-structures.
P.1.20 Predictions for K0
The theory predicts:
• no observable dynamics at K0 ,
• universality of thresholds for all levels,
• inevitability of dimensional growth under metapressure,
• existence of meta-ontological branching structures.
P.1.21 Experiments for K0
K0 cannot be experimentally probed directly. Indirect tests:
• universality of threshold behaviour across physical, chemical, biological, cognitive and social systems,
• ubiquity of structural recursion patterns,
• falsifiability tests of emergent time (Physics Run),
• stability of branching structures (K11 –K12 ).
P.1.22 Collapse and Death of K0
Collapse occurs if:
Ω(K0 ) = ∅.
This corresponds to:
• contradictory meta-laws,
• logically inconsistent possibility space,
• unsupportable recursion Ψ or Φ,
• violation of Θcoh or Θadm .
If K0 collapses, all continua collapse simultaneously.
P.1.23 Falsifiability of K0
The following predictions are falsifiable:
1. Universal presence of thresholds Θ across all levels.
2. Irreversibility of dimensional growth (Theorem 1).
3. Emergence of time only at K2 through cycles.
4. Existence of universal recursion Kx → Mx → Kx+1 .
Failure of any of these behaviours empirically falsifies K0 .
194

P.1.24 Branching / Ontological Position of K0
Based on Axiom 21 (Ontological Branching), K0 is the root node of the ontological branching tree:
K0 → K1 → K2 → · · · → K12 .
All branches must remain compatible with L; incompatible branches die through collapse of admissibility.
P.1.25 Relation to M-spaces
K0 defines the admissibility and structure of all meta-spaces:
Mx ⊆ Ω(K0 ).
Conversely:
K x ⊆ Mx ,

Mx ⊆ Ω(Kx+1 ),

which makes K0 the single unifying superspace for the entire hierarchy.
P.1.26 K1 Overview
Level K1 is the first genuinely structural continuum. It arises from the action of the operator Ψ0→1 on K0 ,
introducing a one-dimensional axis A1 and thus enabling the existence of continuous degrees of freedom.
K1 is not yet physical space; rather, it is the abstract prototype of a one-dimensional continuum:
K1 = (X, τ, µ, A1 ),
where X is a one-dimensional domain, τ is the structural topology, and µ is a measure compatible with
τ.
The creation of K1 is the first step where:
• differences can be expressed along an axis,
• coherent variation becomes possible,
• structural tension can propagate,
• constraints produce continuous curves.
Every higher continuum inherits A1 as its foundational axis.
P.1.27 State Space Ω(K1 )
The state space of K1 is:
Ω(K1 ) = C 0 (X, V ),
the space of continuous functions from the one-dimensional domain X to a value set V .
Properties:
1. Ω(K1 ) is infinite-dimensional (function space).
2. Every configuration is continuous by definition.
3. Discontinuities lie outside Ω(K1 ) and correspond to violations of structural coherence.
4. X may be open, closed, compact or non-compact depending on constraints in the corresponding
M1 .
This is the minimal space in which continuous variation exists.
195

P.1.28 Boundary ∂Ω(K1 )
The boundary consists of configurations that approach loss of continuity:
∂Ω(K1 ) = {f ∈ C 0 (X, V ) : ∃ x0 ∈ X with lim f (x) undefined}.
x→x0

Interpretation:
• Points where continuity fails.
• Points where structural tension exceeds Θ1 .
• Points where the domain X degenerates or collapses.
Crossing the boundary destroys the continuum K1 .
P.1.29 Axes A(K1 )
K1 has exactly one axis:
A1 : X → R,
representing the intrinsic parameter along which differences become ordered.
Conditions:
• A1 must be monotonic (Axiom A1,mon ).
• A1 must be connected (Axiom A1,conn ).
• A1 must allow variation compatible with τ .
All future axes Ak for k ≥ 2 extend this foundational structure.
P.1.30 Potentials P (K1 )
Potentials on K1 include:
P (K1 ) = {Pgrad , Pbound , Psmooth },
describing:
• gradients along the axis,
• boundary-induced stresses,
• smoothness constraints,
• allowed curvature of functions in Ω(K1 ).
These are not yet forces; they are structural potentials governing coherence of variation.
P.1.31 Thresholds Θ(K1 )
Thresholds regulate the admissibility of states:
Θ(K1 ) = {Θcont , Θgrad , Θsmooth }.
Examples:
• Θcont — minimal continuity required.
• Θgrad — maximal admissible gradient before tension becomes unsustainable.
• Θsmooth — minimal regularity required.
If any threshold is exceeded, the configuration lies outside Ω(K1 ).

196

P.1.32 Flows J(K1 )
Flows describe allowed continuous changes along A1 :
J(K1 ) = {∂x f (x), ∂t f (x, t), admissible deformations}.
Key properties:
• flows propagate structural tension,
• flows must preserve continuity,
• flows cannot create new axes (requires K1 → K2 transition).
P.1.33 Cycles C(K1 )
Because K1 supports continuous variation but not yet multi-dimensional interaction, cycles are topologically trivial:
Ctriv = constant loops in function space.
No nontrivial structural cycles exist, since cyclic structure requires at least two independent axes (K2 ).
Thus:
τ (K1 ) cannot emerge.
P.1.34 Time τ (K1 )
Time does not exist at K1 .
According to the Time-Origin Theorem (Physics Run):
time emerges only at K2 from non-degradable cycles.
Thus:
τ (K1 ) is undefined and unrepresentable.

k(K1 ) measures whether K1 remains structurally viable.
P.1.36 Structural Tension T (K1 )
Structural tension on K1 arises from:
• gradients of functions,
• boundary effects,
• incompatibility of constraints along A1 .

P.1.38 Operators on K1 (Ψ, Φ, Λ, U , X)
• Ψ1→2 — birth of the second axis A2 , enabling K2 .
• Φ — evolution of the admissible meta-space M1 .
• Λ — constraint operator enforcing continuity, monotonicity and connectedness.
• U — unification of local structure into global coherence.
• X — branching operator enabling incompatible K1 manifolds.
These operators define how K1 evolves and how new dimensions arise.
P.1.39 Processes on K1
Key processes:
• propagation of gradients,
• smoothing of discontinuities,
• stabilization of continuous configurations,
• structural collapse under excessive tension,
• dimensional transition to K2 under pressure of incompatible differences (Axiom 15).
P.1.40 Predictions for K1
The theory predicts:
1. continuity must be globally maintained;
2. dimensional growth requires incompatible variations that cannot be represented on a single axis;
3. no temporal phenomena appear at K1 ;
4. collapse under excessive gradients is universal;
5. all K1 continua must embed into their M1 meta-space.

198

P.1.41 Experiments for K1
Indirect tests:
• universality of 1D gradient-collapse behaviour in physical, chemical and biological filaments,
• observation of threshold behaviour under steep gradients,
• detection of forced dimensional growth in systems where a single axis becomes insuﬀicient.
Examples:
• polymer strand collapse under tension,
• memristive filament breakdown,
• 1D reaction-diffusion channel instability.
P.1.42 Collapse and Death of K1
K1 collapses when:
Ω(K1 ) = ∅.
This happens if:
• continuity is broken,
• gradients exceed thresholds,
• constraints in L (carried from K0 ) become incompatible.
After collapse, transition to K2 is impossible.
P.1.43 Falsifiability of K1
Predictions that may be empirically falsified:
1. universal presence of continuity thresholds,
2. absence of nontrivial cycles,
3. absence of emergent time,
4. monotonic connected axis requirement,
5. dimensional transition only under incompatible differences.
Violation of any of these predictions challenges the K1 description.
P.1.44 Branching / Ontological Position of K1
K1 sits directly above K0 in the ontological tree:
K0 → K1 → K2 .
Branching at K1 corresponds to incompatible admissible manifolds sharing the same meta-laws but
differing in structural constraints.
Such branches remain admissible as long as they stay within Ω(K1 ).

199

P.1.45 Relation to M-spaces
K1 is embedded in its meta-space:
K1 ⊆ M1 ⊆ Ω(K0 ).
M1 determines:
• the topology τ of X,
• the regularity constraints,
• permissible ranges for potentials,
• admissibility thresholds.
The transition to K2 occurs when:
A1 cannot represent all emerging differences.
P.1.46 K2 Overview
Level K2 is the first continuum that supports genuine two-dimensional structure. It arises through the
dimensional transition Ψ1→2 when the constraints of K1 become insuﬀicient to represent incompatible
variations (Axiom 15). The new axis A2 is orthogonal in the structural sense and cannot be expressed as
a function of A1 .
As a result, K2 becomes the first level at which:
• nontrivial cycles exist,
• time τ emerges (via stable C-cycles),
• gradients and potentials form two-dimensional fields,
• defects, vortices and dislocations appear,
• topological phenomena become meaningful.
K2 is the minimal setting for classical field-theoretic behaviour and the BKT-type transition.
P.1.47 State Space Ω(K2 )
The state space of K2 is:
Ω(K2 ) = C 0 (X1 × X2 , V ),
a space of continuous fields over a 2D domain.
Key properties:
1. Ω(K2 ) contains configurations with meaningful local gradients in two independent directions.
2. Defects (e.g., vortices) lie in ∂Ω(K2 ) unless they satisfy admissibility constraints of M2 .
3. Nontrivial homotopy classes exist:
π1 (Ω(K2 )) 6= 0.
This is the first level where geometry (in the weak structural sense) emerges.

200

P.1.48 Boundary ∂Ω(K2 )
∂Ω(K2 ) contains:
• discontinuous fields,
• fields whose energy density diverges,
• configurations exceeding Θgrad or Θdefect ,
• fields where cycles collapse (C → ∅).
A special part of the boundary corresponds to topological defects whose core size collapses to zero,
signalling destruction of dimensional coherence.
P.1.49 Axes A(K2 )
Axes consist of:
A(K2 ) = {A1 , A2 },
where:
• A1 is inherited from K1 ,
• A2 is a new independent structural axis.
The independence condition is:
∄ h : R → R such that A2 = h ◦ A1 .
This independence is the formal core of the dimensional jump.
P.1.50 Potentials P (K2 )
The set of potentials now includes full 2D structural terms:
P (K2 ) = {Pgrad , Pcurl , Pdiv , Pbond , Psmooth , Ptop }.
Interpretation:
• gradients in two axes encode local tension,
• curl-like structures encode rotational degrees of freedom,
• divergence potentials encode compressive or dilational tension,
• Ptop captures energy of vortices and defects.
These potentials reproduce, at the abstract level, the structural precursors of fields in physics.
P.1.51 Thresholds Θ(K2 )
Thresholds now include:
Θ(K2 ) = {Θgrad , Θcurl , Θdefect , Θcoh , ΘBKT }.
Their meaning:
• Θgrad : maximal admissible gradient magnitude.
• Θcurl : rotational tolerance.
• Θdefect : defect-core stability threshold.
• Θcoh : coherence threshold for 2D order.
• ΘBKT : threshold for the appearance of stable C-cycles; equivalent to Kc in the BKT theorem of
representability.
Crossing ΘBKT yields the emergent time axis.

• diffusion-like equilibration,
• defect-annihilation and defect-unbinding dynamics.
Flows define the dynamical admissibility of evolution in Ω(K2 ).

P.1.58 Operators on K2 (Ψ, Φ, Λ, U , X)
• Ψ2→3 — dimensional transition to K3 when 2D structure becomes insuﬀicient.
• Φ — meta-space evolution operator for M2 .
• Λ — constraint-enforcing operator that stabilizes gradients, smoothness and defect bounds.
• U — unification of local 2D regions into global coherent fields.
• X — branching operator allowing multiple K2 manifolds with different coherence structures.
P.1.59 Processes on K2
Processes include:
• vortex creation, annihilation and drift,
• phase ordering and disordering,
• BKT-type transitions,
• stabilization of global coherence,

• dimensional growth to K3 when incompatible variations cannot be captured by {A1 , A2 }.

P.1.60 Predictions for K2
1. Existence of a coherence threshold Kc (BKT).
2. Sharp transition between stable and unstable vortices.
3. Emergence of time only when vortex cycles stabilize.
4. Universal power-law correlations below Kc .
5. Loss of coherence under defect proliferation.
6. Necessity of two independent axes for nontrivial cycles.
These predictions match a wide class of physical systems (XY-model, superfluid films, thin magnetic
layers).
P.1.61 Experiments for K2
Canonical experimental signatures:
• measurement of vortex-unbinding temperature in 2D superfluids,
• detection of BKT-like transitions in atomically thin films,
• observation of coherence collapse at high defect density,
• phase-ordering kinetics in 2D materials,
• universal jump in stiffness at the BKT transition.
Indirect tests appear in:
• graphene defect dynamics,
• 2D liquid-crystal films,
• biological membranes with topological defect patterns.
P.1.62 Collapse and Death of K2
K2 collapses when:
Ω(K2 ) = ∅,
due to:
• runaway defect proliferation,
• loss of coherence (T > Θcoh ),
• destruction of all C-cycles,
• inability to maintain two independent axes.
After collapse, no transition to K3 is possible.
P.1.63 Falsifiability of K2
Falsifiable predictions:
1. existence of a sharp BKT-like threshold,
2. necessity of cycles for emergent time,
3. correlation-length behaviour near Kc ,
204

4. universal stiffness jump,
5. topological protection of Cvortex above Kc .
Empirical violation of these features would contradict the structural model.
P.1.64 Branching / Ontological Position of K2
K2 is the root of all higher-dimensional continua:
K0 → K1 → K2 → K3 → . . .
Branching at K2 corresponds to different admissible 2D coherence structures:
• vortex-rich vs vortex-free phases,
• smooth vs defect-dominated manifolds,
• high-coherence vs low-coherence branches.
These branches remain distinct unless unified by operator U .
P.1.65 Relation to M-spaces
K2 is embedded in:
K 2 ⊆ M2 ⊆ M1 ⊆ M0 .
M2 defines:
• admissible 2D topologies,
• allowed defect classes,
• gradient and curl bounds,
• coherence conditions for dimensional stability.
Transition to K3 requires that M2 cannot accommodate new incompatible classes of differences.
P.1.66 K3 Overview
K3 is the level at which chemical organisation becomes structurally possible. It represents the transition
from purely geometric and topological continua (K0 –K2 ) to systems in which:
• reactions, transformations and conversions appear as admissible flows,
• potentials correspond to reaction aﬀinities and concentration gradients,
• boundaries ∂Ω include molecular-compositional and topological constraints,
• minimal autocatalytic closure becomes representable,
• the first structurally coherent networks arise (RAF networks).
The dimensional transition Ψ2→3 occurs when incompatible chemical differences cannot be expressed
within the axes {A1 , A2 } of K2 . A new axis A3 is introduced, representing a distinct dimension of
composition space, enabling emergent chemical continua.
K3 serves as the structural substrate for all later biological and cognitive continua, but itself remains
non-living.

P.1.67 State Space Ω(K3 )

M

Properties:

2. Admissible states must satisfy mass-balance constraints and threshold limitations from M3 .
3. RAF subnetworks embed into Ω(K3 ) as structurally coherent regions.
Stability of K3 depends on whether Ω(K3 ) contains any closed autocatalytic subsets with sustained
flux.
P.1.68 Boundary ∂Ω(K3 )
∂Ω(K3 ) includes:
• states where any concentration becomes negative (forbidden),
• divergent fluxes exceeding Θflux ,
• chemical configurations violating stoichiometric feasibility,
• collapse regimes: pH-collapse, osmotic collapse, reaction-chain instability,
• loss of autocatalytic closure.
Critical for K3 : loss of closure implies Ω(K3 ) becomes disconnected, preventing sustained organisation.
P.1.69 Axes A(K3 )
K3 supports three independent structural axes:
A(K3 ) = {A1 , A2 , A3 },
where A3 is the new compositional axis.
A3 encodes:
• stoichiometric structure,
• reaction-direction degrees of freedom,
• compositional differences that cannot be mapped to geometric or phase-coherence differences of K2 .
Independence:

This expresses the irreducible novelty of chemical organisation.

• Paffinity : reaction driving forces,
• Pmix : entropic mixing potentials,
• Pexchange : exchange with environment (if allowed by M3 ).
Chemical organisation arises when these potentials create a stable, self-reinforcing structure.
P.1.71 Thresholds Θ(K3 )
Relevant thresholds include:
Θ(K3 ) = {Θclosure , Θflux , ΘpH , Θosm , Θgrad , Θreact }.
Interpretation:
• Θclosure : minimal conditions for autocatalytic closure,
• Θflux : maximal sustainable reaction rate,
• ΘpH : permissible acid-base imbalance,
• Θosm : osmotic-stability threshold,
• Θgrad : concentration-gradient bounds,
• Θreact : energy threshold for reactions.
Crossing these thresholds drives collapse (Section P.1.82).
P.1.72 Flows J(K3 )
Admissible flows:

Qualitative types:
• linear mass-action flows,
• nonlinear autocatalytic flows,
• balancing flows preventing runaway instability,
• exchange flows across proto-boundaries.
Autocatalytic flows are central: they define structural amplification necessary for K3 viability.

CRAF is the minimal closed RAF cycle satisfying:

Properties:
• RAF cycles provide structural persistence,
• their power functional Π(CRAF ) determines whether organisation is sustainable,
• existence of CRAF is necessary (but not suﬀicient) for transition to K4 .
When CRAF becomes stable, K3 supports precursor forms of temporal ordering.
P.1.74 Time τ (K3 )
Time in K3 arises when autocatalytic cycles maintain non-zero cycle power:
τ (K3 ) exists iff Π(CRAF ) > Θtime .
Temporal structure is weaker than in K2 :
• time is defined through reaction-cycle iteration,
• time fails if cycles extinguish or drift to zero flux.
Stable temporal ordering is a necessary condition for transition to biological K4 .

P.1.86 K4 Overview
K4 is the level where a biological structure first becomes possible. The defining event is the appearance
of a semi-stable membrane that generates a new ontological distinction:
inside | outside.
This is a genuine new axis of the continuum, creating:
• a bounded chemical interior,
• selective transport regimes,
• spatially structured gradients,
• proto-homeostasis,
• the first biological cycles of excitation, survival and repair.
The transition K3 → K4 corresponds to protocell formation: a RAF network enclosed by a semipermeable membrane whose stability is governed by threshold conditions Θmem , Θperm , Θosm and Θcurv .
K4 is the minimal biological continuum: the simplest form of organised and sustained protocellular
life.
P.1.87 State Space Ω(K4 )
The state space includes:
Ω(K4 ) = {(cin , cout , ∂Ω, g, ΓRAF , p)},
where:
• cin : concentrations inside the membrane,
• cout : external concentrations,
• ∂Ω: membrane boundary with patch-structure,
• g: gradients across the membrane (osmotic, ionic, pH, potential),
• ΓRAF : the internal catalytic network,
• p: permeability and curvature parameters for each boundary patch.
The state space is higher-dimensional than K3 due to membrane topology and patchwise degrees of
freedom.
Admissible states must satisfy:
• membrane cohesion,

211

• controlled permeability,
• non-destructive gradients,
• viability of RAF network inside.

These axes are not reducible to chemical axes of K3 ; each represents new structural differences of
biological organisation.

P.1.106 K5 Overview
K5 is the level at which electrical excitability emerges as a new ontological dimension. The protocell
boundary of K4 becomes an electrically active membrane through the formation of ion channels with
controlled conductance. This generates a new axis:
Aexc : ∆V 7→ electrical state difference,
where ∆V is the transmembrane potential.
This axis is not definable in K4 . It represents a new class of incompatible differences and therefore
constitutes a genuine increase in dimension.
Organisationally, K5 is characterised by:
• stable ion channels (open/closed/leaky/blocked),
• controlled ionic fluxes,
• excitable cycles (excitation–recovery),
• refractory dynamics,
• noise control and thresholded responses,
• self-sustaining electrical organisation tightly coupled to the chemical interior.
K5 is the minimal neuron-like continuum, even if no real neurons exist yet.
P.1.107 State Space Ω(K5 )
A state of K5 includes:
Ω(K5 ) = {∆V, ci , gion , Popen , x(t), G = (V, E), I(t)}.
Components:
• ∆V — transmembrane potential,
• ci — ionic concentrations inside and outside,
• gion — conductances of ion channels,
• Popen — open probabilities,
217

• x(t) — internal activation variables,
• G = (V, E) — proto-neural connectivity graph for multi-unit K5 systems,
• I(t) — external or internal currents.
Admissibility requires:
|∆V | < Θvolt−max ,

ci ∈ viability range,

0 ≤ Popen ≤ 1.

P.1.108 Boundary ∂Ω(K5 )
The membrane inherits K4 ’s boundary with a new structure:
∂Ω(K5 ) = ∂Ω(K4 ) ∪ {ion channels with gating kinetics}.
For each channel k:
• state space: open/closed/blocked/leaky,
• parameters: gk , reversal potential Ek , gating variables,
• patch-level localisation,
• interactions with local curvature and tension.
Collapse of channel ordering or gating kinetics destroys Ω(K5 ).
P.1.109 Axes A(K5 )
The minimal axes are:
A(K5 ) = A(K4 ) ∪ {Aexc , Aion , Agate }.
Where:
• Aexc : electrical excitation axis,
• Aion : ionic species and flux differences,
• Agate : gating-state differences for ion channels.
These axes are incompatible with chemical-only differences of K4 and imply a higher-dimensional
continuum.
P.1.110 Potentials P (K5 )
Potentials include:
P (K5 ) = {Eion , Pgate , Pexc , Pnoise , Prefrac , Pcoupling }.
Interpretation:
• Eion — Nernst potentials for each ionic species,
• Pgate — gating activation potentials,
• Pexc — excitation thresholds for spike initiation,
• Pnoise — noise-control potentials,
• Prefrac — refractory resetting potentials,
• Pcoupling — potentials for electrically coupling multiple units via G.

P.1.111 Thresholds Θ(K5 )

Θ(K5 ) = {Θexc , Θnoise , Θvolt−max , Θchannel−open , Θchannel−close , Θchannel−noise , Θfront , Θrefrac }.
Meaning:
• Θexc : excitation threshold for spike generation,
• Θnoise : noise limit beyond which excitation is lost,
• Θvolt−max : maximal safe transmembrane voltage,
• Θchannel−open , Θchannel−close : gating viability thresholds,
• Θchannel−noise : noise tolerance in gating,
• Θfront : minimal conditions for propagation fronts in multi-unit settings,
• Θrefrac : minimal refractory recovery level.
Exceeding Θvolt−max or Θchannel−noise annihilates the continuum.
P.1.112 Flows J(K5 )
Flows:
• ionic currents:
Jion,k = gk (∆V − Ek ),
• leak currents and noise currents,
• gating-variable flows: ẋ = f (x, ∆V ),
• spike-propagation flows over graph edges E,
• refractoriness recovery flows,
• coupling flows between units.
Stability requires:
σ(J) < σmax (K5 ).
P.1.113 Cycles C(K5 )
Characteristic cycles:
C(K5 ) = {Cexc , Crefrac , Cnoise−control , Cchannel−dynamics , Ccoupling }.
Descriptions:
• Cexc : excitation cycle (rest → excitation → peak → repolarisation),
• Crefrac : refractory cycle restoring channel states,
• Cnoise−control : suppression of stochastic fluctuations,
• Cchannel−dynamics : gating cycles that sustain excitability,
• Ccoupling : multi-unit synchronisation cycles.
Each cycle has a characteristic period τCj .

P.1.118 Operators on K5 (Ψ, Φ, Λ, U , X)
• Ψ5→6 — emergence of cognitive modelling axes and transformation of excitation cycles into attractors,

• Λ — structural coupling of excitation with chemical homeostasis,

P.1.119 Processes on K5

• spike initiation and recovery,

P.1.120 Predictions for K5
1. Excitability requires tightly controlled noise regimes.
2. Spike-like events appear spontaneously once Θexc is crossed.
3. Global depolarisation causes structural collapse.
4. Networked K5 systems form attractors that prefigure K6 cognitive models.
5. Channel diversity expands viable regions of Ω(K5 ).
P.1.121 Experiments for K5
Empirical analogues:
• artificial lipid vesicles with reconstituted ion channels,

• voltage-clamp characterisation of ∆V thresholds,

• proto-neuron models with minimal excitability.
These tests directly probe Θexc , Θnoise , Θchannel−open , etc.

P.1.122 Collapse and Death of K5
Occurs when:
Ω(K5 ) = ∅.
Mechanisms:
• uncontrolled depolarisation,
• channel malfunction or gating collapse,
• ionic-gradient dissipation,
• noise-induced runaway failures,
• inability to recover from excitation.
Collapse prevents emergence of K6 .
P.1.123 Falsifiability of K5
Key testable predictions:
1. Excitable behaviour cannot be sustained without refractory cycles.
2. Noise-control thresholds are real and measurable.
3. Ion-channel distributions determine viability boundaries.
4. Stable attractors in K5 must exist before K6 can form.
5. Spike propagation requires Θfront .
Failure of these predictions refutes the model of K5 .
P.1.124 Branching / Ontological Position of K5
Branching types:
• tonic–phasic–burst excitability regimes,
• multi-channel vs. single-channel systems,
• weakly vs. strongly coupled units,
• distributed vs. localised excitation patterns.
Ontological location:
K4 → K5 → K6 .
K5 is the bridge between biological protocells and cognitive systems.
P.1.125 Relation to M-spaces
M5 specifies:
• permitted ionic species and charge-carriers,
• admissible ranges of conductances and potentials,
• noise regimes compatible with excitability,
• environmental constraints allowing channel stability,
• allowed coupling structures.
Compatibility of K5 with M5 determines the existence of electrically excitable systems.
222

P.1.126 K6 Overview
K6 is the level at which cognitive organisation emerges as an ontological dimension. The excitable
electrical dynamics of K5 produce stable attractors; these attractors become models that encode internal
structure, memory, predictive states and representational relations.
The birth of K6 occurs when excitation cycles of K5 are no longer merely electrical waves, but become
informationally interpretable patterns whose differences cannot be expressed in A(K5 ). This necessitates
a new set of axes and a new dimensional structure.
The minimal features:
• representational states,
• prediction capability (prediction error axis),
• semantic and binding structure,
• internal models µt ,
• memory consolidation/reconsolidation,
• stable components of cognitive graphs,
• emergence of proto-symbols.
K6 is the smallest continuum that deserves the name “cognitive”. It is not yet linguistic or social
(those belong to K7 ).
P.1.127 State Space Ω(K6 )
A state of K6 is:
Ω(K6 ) = {m, µt , Gcog , x(t), ri , P Et , Bt , Mcon , Mrec }.
Elements:
• m — active cognitive model,
• µt — distribution of model states,
• Gcog — cognitive graph (nodes = models, edges = binding),
• x(t) — activation patterns inherited from K5 attractors,
• ri — representational units (proto-symbols),
• P Et — prediction error,
• Bt — binding configuration,
• Mcon , Mrec — consolidated vs. reconsolidating memory states.
Admissibility:
D(m) ≤ Θcog ,

|P Et | < Θpred ,

D(m) is inconsistency of model m.
P.1.128 Boundary ∂Ω(K6 )
Cognitive boundaries include:
• limits of representational capacity,
• edges of binding depth,
• maximal prediction-horizon,
223

Bt ∈ binding-capacity.

• memory stability limits,
• semantic coherence boundaries,
• transitions where P Et cannot be reconciled.
Crossing ∂Ω(K6 ) collapses modelling capability.
P.1.129 Axes A(K6 )
As established in K6 Run 2, the minimal set is:
A(K6 ) = {Asel , Acmp , Abind , Acat , Amem , Apred , Amodel }.
Interpretation:
• Asel — selection axis (which model is active),
• Acmp — comparison axis,
• Abind — binding axis (feature composition),
• Acat — categorisation axis,
• Amem — memory axis,
• Apred — prediction axis,
• Amodel — model-identity axis.
These axes cannot be reduced to excitation differences of K5 .
P.1.130 Potentials P (K6 )
Potentials regulate artefacts of cognition:
P (K6 ) = {Ppred , Pval , Pbind , Psal , Pmem , Pelim }.
Where:
• Ppred — prediction potential controlling model update,
• Pval — valence potential (affective shaping),
• Pbind — potential for feature binding,
• Psal — salience modulation,
• Pmem — consolidation pressure for memory,
• Pelim — elimination of incoherent models.
P.1.131 Thresholds Θ(K6 )
Thresholds determine cognitive viability:
Θ(K6 ) = {Θcog , Θpred , Θbind , Θsal , Θmodel , Θmem−stab , Θnoise−cog }.
Meaning:
• Θcog : global inconsistency tolerance,
• Θpred : maximal allowable prediction error,
• Θbind : binding capacity limit,
224

• Θsal : saturation threshold for salience,
• Θmodel : collapse limit for model viability,
• Θmem−stab : memory stability threshold,
• Θnoise−cog : cognitive noise tolerance.
Crossing these leads to K6 collapse or transition to K7 depending on direction.
P.1.132 Flows J(K6 )
The flows are informational and representational:
• Jpred = −∇m P Et — prediction update flow,
• Jbind — binding/unbinding transitions,
• Jcmp — comparison dynamics,
• Jsel — model-selection flow,
• Jmem — consolidation/reconsolidation flow,
• Jelim — elimination of incoherent models.
Stability requires:
σ(Jpred ) < σmax (K6 ).
P.1.133 Cycles C(K6 )
Characteristic cycles include:
C(K6 ) = {Cpred , Cbind , Cmem , Ccmp , Cmodel }.
Descriptions:
• Cpred : prediction cycle (model → prediction → error → update),
• Cbind : feature-binding cycle (composition → stabilisation → release),
• Cmem : memory cycle (consolidation → storage → reconsolidation),
• Ccmp : comparison–differentiation cycle,
• Cmodel : cycle of model selection, evaluation, elimination.
Each has characteristic period τCj .
P.1.134 Time τ (K6 )
Time arises from stability of cognitive cycles:
τ (K6 ) = min τCj ,
j

Π(Cj ) > Θtime .

Cognitive time is slower and more integrative than electrical time (K5 ).

P.1.143 Falsifiability of K6

P.1.146 K7 Overview
K7 is the level of social continua: systems whose states, axes and potentials arise from interaction between
multiple K6 cognitive continua. It is the smallest level at which:
• shared models and common knowledge emerge,
• communication forms a structural dimension,
• cooperation and conflict become dynamical forces,
• social identity and role formation appear,
• collective memory and norms stabilise behaviour,
• group-level cycles define temporal organisation.
K7 is not a sum of agents: it is a new continuum with its own admissible states, thresholds, flows and
death mechanisms.
P.1.147 State Space Ω(K7 )
A state of the social continuum includes:
(7)

Ω(K7 ) = {Gsoc , Mshared , Ccomm , Rroles , Nnorms , Hhist , Sstruc , µt , Σidentity }.
Components:
• Gsoc — social graph (agents as nodes, ties as edges),
• Mshared — shared models (collective beliefs),
• Ccomm — communication structure,
• Rroles — role allocation (statuses, functions),
• Nnorms — norms and constraints,
• Hhist — collective histories and narratives,
• Sstruc — structural positions and modules,
(7)

• µt

— distribution of group states over time,

• Σidentity — social identity structures.
Admissibility is constrained by M7 and group-coherence thresholds.
P.1.148 Boundary ∂Ω(K7 )
The boundary includes:
• collapse of shared models,
• fragmentation of the social graph,
• breakdown of communication,
• loss of normative coherence,
• role instability,
• identity collapse,
• inability to stabilise collective memory.
Crossing ∂Ω(K7 ) destroys group continuity.

P.2 MSpaces
The family of meta-spaces M0 , M1 , . . . , M12 provides the admissibility structure for continua K0 . . . K12 .
Each Ki can exist only if its full configuration Ω(Ki ) lies strictly within the admissible region of the
corresponding meta-space Mi :
Ω(Ki ) ⊆ Ω(Mi ).
M-spaces have three universal functions:
1. Admissibility constraints: they define which structural configurations, thresholds and flows are
permitted. They serve as the global regulator of continua.
2. Dimensional guidance: Mi+1 determines whether Ki can form new axes and transition into a
higher-dimensional continuum.
3. Structural supervision: each meta-space enforces global compatibility of operators such as Ψ,
Φ, Λ, U , and X, and ensures that continua obey the universal laws of evolution, collapse, and
branching.
M-spaces do not evolve “inside” the K-hierarchy; instead, they form a parallel supervisory structure.
The relation can be visualised as:
Ki ,→ Mi ,

Mi ⇒ constraints on Ki .

The transition Ki → Ki+1 is possible only if:
A(Ki+1 ) ⊆ A(Mi+1 ),

P (Ki+1 ) ⊆ P (Mi+1 ),

Θ(Ki+1 ) ≤ Θ(Mi+1 ).

Each Mi expands the dimensionality of admissible structures compared to Mi−1 , providing the overstructure within which the next continuum level may emerge.
P.2.1 M1 Overview
M1 is the meta-space that provides the admissibility structure for the one-dimensional continuum K1 . Unlike M0 , which governs only proto-differences, M1 introduces the first genuine geometric and dynamical
admissibility conditions:
Ω(K1 ) ⊆ Ω(M1 ).
M1 is the minimal meta-space in which the following are well-defined:
• a measurable axis A1 ;
• a continuous field φ(x) over a one-dimensional domain;
• proto-dynamics via flows J1 = (∂x φ, ∂t φ);
• admissible energy functionals and actions;
• well-formed structural tension T1 and a meaningful threshold Θ1 ;
• the existence and collapse rules of K1 .
Thus, M1 is the meta-structure that makes K1 mathematically and physically possible.

• oscillatory axes without admissible dynamics.

P.2.3 M3 Overview
M3 is the meta-space that provides the admissibility conditions for three-dimensional continua K3 . It is
the first meta-space in which:
• a third independent axis A3 becomes admissible,
• reactive structure appears (chemical binding / dissociation),
• valence states become part of the admissible configuration space,
• diffusion and transport occur in three spatial dimensions,
• local interaction graphs (reaction networks) are stable objects,
• activation thresholds and reaction potentials become well-defined,
• spatial heterogeneity and gradients are dynamically supported.
M3 is the mathematical and physical environment within which the chemical continuum K3 can exist,
evolve and undergo structural transitions towards higher continua such as K4 .
1. Admissible Configuration Space Ω(M3 )
The admissible set of configurations in M3 is:
o
n
Ω(M3 ) = (φ, Gchem , ρ, gij ) φ ∈ C 0 (X3 , V ), Gchem ∈ GRAF , ρ ∈ L1 (X3 ), gij ∈ C 0 .
Key admissibility conditions:
1. Three-dimensional topology. X3 must be a 3-manifold supporting local coordinate charts, differentiability and diffusion.
2. Local reaction networks. Gchem must be representable as a finite, locally supported reaction graph
satisfying the RAF conditions for closure and catalytic action.
3. Density fields. ρ(x) defines molecular or atomic concentrations and must be integrable with finite
total mass.
4. Metric admissibility. gij describes spatial geometry but does not yet include relativistic structure;
only Riemannian (positive definite) metrics are admissible at this level.
5. Locality. All interactions must be expressible through local potentials and local reaction kernels.
Thus, Ω(M3 ) expands the geometric and physical admissibility of M2 into the chemical regime.
2. Admissible Axes A(M3 )
A new axis A3 becomes admissible in M3 , satisfying:
A3 6⊂ span(A1 , A2 ),

T2 ≥ Θdim .

Additional admissible internal axes:
• Aval : valence states (bonding possibilities),
• Areact : admissible reaction modes,
• Aconf : configuration states of molecules.
These internal axes encode chemical structure within the meta-space.

P.3 Cross-level structures
P.3.1 Purpose of the Cross-K layer
The Cross-K layer formalises all structures, transitions and constraints that link different continuum levels
K0 → K12 . While each K-level has its own ontology (axes, potentials, thresholds, flows, cycles, domains
Ω(K), boundaries ∂Ω(K) and continuum measure k(K)), many phenomena in the Core require relations
across levels. These relations are neither optional nor external: they are part of the intrinsic architecture
of a dynamic continuum.
The Cross-K layer therefore:
• defines mapping structures between levels;
• specifies transition operators and their constraints;
• introduces consistency conditions ensuring that evolution across adjacent levels is mathematically
and conceptually valid;
• provides global landscape rules, describing how the entire stack of K-levels forms a coherent metacontinuum.
P.3.2 Definition of Cross-K structures
A Cross-K structure is any formal object that:
1. involves at least two levels Ki , Kj with i 6= j;
2. establishes a relation Rij between their components (A, P, Θ, J, C, Ω, ∂Ω, k);
3. satisfies the general compatibility rule:
Rij : Ki ↔ Kj
while preserving continuity and allowing valid transitions under the global operator E.
Thus Cross-K structures include:
• transition maps (dimensional, structural, energetic);
• inheritance relations (axes, potentials, thresholds);
• boundary transformations between ∂Ω(Ki ) and ∂Ω(Kj );
• cycle projections and lifts (mapping cycles from one level into another);
• global constraints ensuring that no level violates the rules of its neighbours.

298

P.3.3 Role of this master file
This master module intentionally remains a thin orchestration layer. It does not store heavy theoretical
content. Instead, it:
• introduces the concept of Cross-K structures,
• provides the global definition and purpose,
• and assembles all detailed cross-level analyses through \input.
The individual transition sections are organised as:
• global landscape (all-level perspective),
• local transitions (Ki → Ki+1 ),
• special two-way or non-adjacent mappings where required.
P.3.4 Module structure
The following files are orchestrated by this module:
• crossk_global_landscape.tex — global multi-level geometry;
• crossk_k0_k1.tex, crossk_k1_k2.tex, …— adjacent-level transition blocks;
• crossk_k10_k11.tex, crossk_k11_k12.tex — upper-level transitions and meta-structures.
P.3.5 Inclusion of detailed sections
The detailed cross-K analyses can be included as:
\input{content/crossk/crossk_global_landscape.tex}
\input{content/crossk/crossk_k0_k1.tex}
\input{content/crossk/crossk_k1_k2.tex}
...
\input{content/crossk/crossk_k11_k12.tex}
This file thus defines the conceptual container for the Cross-K domain of OC Core 1.3.
P.3.6 Global cross-K landscape
The cross-K landscape describes how individual continua Kd are embedded into a single multi-level
structure. Instead of treating each level as an isolated theory, the Ontology of Continua organises them
as a chain of dimension-increasing transitions:
Rd : Kd → Kd+1 ,
where each Rd is a constrained transition that:
• preserves the core axioms (non-emptiness of Ω, thresholds, flows, cycles),
• introduces at least one new axis Anew ∈ Md \ A(Kd ),
• passes a dimensional threshold Td > Θd,dim ,
• produces a strictly richer space of admissible states Ω(Kd+1 ) ⊃ Ω(Kd ).
The global landscape is therefore not a flat list of levels, but a structured sequence of phase transitions
in which each Kd emerges from a predecessor and constrains its successors.

299

P.3.7 1. Levels involved and their roles
At a coarse resolution, the chain can be grouped into four bands:
1. Physical band (K0 –K2 ): basic structure, action and percolation of connectivity.
2. Material and biological band (K3 –K5 ): fields, chemistry, compartments and proto-neural dynamics.
3. Cognitive and social band (K6 –K8 ): meaning, social systems and civilisational infrastructures.
4. Theoretical band (K9 –K11 ): theories, metatheories and trans-metatheoretical constraints.
Each band is internally coherent but also linked by explicit cross-level operators Rd and by shared
meta-spaces Mn .
P.3.8 2. Shared axes and thresholds across levels
Across the chain K0 –K11 , several structural motifs reappear:
• Axes A(Kd ): each level introduces new axes but inherits transformed versions of earlier ones (e.g.
energy, gradients, information, roles, symbols).
• Thresholds Θ(Kd ): existence, stability, critical, death and dimensional thresholds appear at all levels,
specialised to the local physics/biology/social/theoretical context.
• State domains Ω(Kd ): every continuum has a non-empty domain of admissible states, with a boundary ∂Ω(Kd ) defined by violated thresholds.
• Cycles C(Kd ): minimal stabilising cycles exist on each level (from trivial physical cycles to institutional and meta-theoretical cycles).
The global landscape can be seen as the evolution of these structural motifs as dimension and complexity increase.
P.3.9 3. Cross-level flows, cycles, and tensions
Cross-level dynamics can be summarised by three families of objects:
Flows. Cross-level flows Jd,d+1 map states and structures from Kd to Kd+1 (e.g. chemical gradients
shaping K4 , neural patterns inducing K6 , social norms supporting K8 ).
Cycles. Some cycles explicitly span multiple levels, such as civilisation–theory feedback loops (K8 –K9 –
K8 ) or meta-theory–practice cycles (K9 –K10 –K8 ).
Tension. Cross-level tension Td,d+1 measures mismatch between the constraints of Kd and Kd+1 ; excessive tension can prevent the birth of a new level or trigger collapse downwards.
Formally, one can write a generic cross-level tension functional

Td,d+1 = F A(Kd+1 ) − A(Kd ), P (Kd+1 ) − P (Kd ), Jd,d+1 , Θ(Kd+1 ) − Θ(Kd ) ,
with Td,d+1 > Θd,dim signalling a dimensional transition.

300

P.3.10 4. Birth and death conditions in the global chain
Birth of a new level Kd+1 is governed by three conditions:
1. Availability of a new axis: there exists Anew ∈ Md such that Anew ∈
/ A(Kd ).
2. Dimensional tension: structural tension exceeds a critical threshold, Td > Θd,dim , making the old
configuration unstable without a new dimension.
3. Admissible state extension: the new domain satisfies Ω(Kd+1 ) 6= ∅ and Ω(Kd+1 ) ⊃ Ω(Kd ).
Death of a level Kd may occur locally (collapse of a specific continuum) or globally (destruction of
its entire class) when:
Ω(Kd ) = ∅

or k(Kd ) → 0

or τcycle (Kd ) → ∞.

Global collapse of multiple adjacent levels can be understood as a cascade of threshold violations
propagating across the chain.
P.3.11 5. Canonical cross-level chains
Several cross-level chains are of particular importance:
• Physical–chemical–biological chain: K1 → K2 → K3 → K4 → K5 (from action and percolation
to membranes and proto-neural dynamics).
• Biological–cognitive–social chain: K4 → K5 → K6 → K7 (from gradients and spikes to cognition
and institutions).
• Social–civilisational–theoretical chain: K7 → K8 → K9 → K10 → K11 (from norms and roles
to civilisational technologies and meta-frameworks).
The detailed cross-K modules in the technical derivation atlas refine these canonical chains by providing explicit descriptions of shared axes, thresholds, flows, cycles and death conditions for each adjacent
transition.
In this sense, the global cross-K landscape is the map of how all individual continua Kd fit into a
single, coherent, multi-level structure.
P.3.12 K0–K1 cross-level structure
The transition from K0 to K1 represents the first and most fundamental cross-level structure in the entire
hierarchy of continua. It describes the birth of distinguishable states, the appearance of an explicit axis,
and the formation of a non-trivial state space Ω(K1 ) from the minimal pre-ontological substrate of K0 .
This section summarises the structural dependencies, inherited components, transition operators, and
threshold conditions for the emergence of K1 .
P.3.13 1. Levels involved and their roles
K0. K0 is defined by the axiom of difference and connectedness. It contains:
• a minimal domain of potential states without explicit axes;
• a structural difference measure ∆(s1 , s2 );
• the existence threshold Θ0 ensuring non-triviality: 0 < ∆ < ε for some ε > 0;
• no time, no flows J, no cycles C, no dynamics.

301

K1. K1 is the first continuum with:
• an explicit axis A1 capturing a stable class of distinctions;
• a defined state space Ω(K1 ) with boundary ∂Ω(K1 );
• a primitive energy/potential structure P1 ;
• minimal flows J1 and a trivial cycle Ctriv ;
• explicit thresholds Θ1 (existence, gradient, stability).
The role of the K0→K1 transition is the generation of structure: the formation of the first representable dimension in the continuum.
P.3.14 2. Shared and inherited axes and thresholds
Although K0 has no axes, several of its structural properties are inherited by K1 in transformed form:
Difference ∆. The primitive difference structure of K0 becomes the metric component of the axis A1
in K1 :
A1 ∼ f (∆),
meaning that the existence of distinguishability in K0 is what enables the emergence of an explicit coordinate in K1 .
Thresholds. The existence threshold Θ0 becomes a lower bound on K1 : if Θ0 fails (i.e., ∆ = 0), then
no axis can be created and Ω(K1 ) = ∅.
Conversely, Θ1 introduces new stability conditions for gradients, boundaries, and allowable flows.
These thresholds do not exist in K0 and are born only after the first axis appears.
P.3.15 3. Cross-level flows, cycles, and tensions
Flows. There are no intrinsic flows in K0 , so the operator J1 of K1 has no precursor. Instead, it arises
from the newly available structure:
J1 : A1 → Ω(K1 )
represents movements along or across the new axis.
Cycles. K0 cannot support cycles because it lacks time and flows. Thus the trivial cycle of K1 :
Ctriv : s 7→ s,
is the first possible cyclic structure in the hierarchy.
Tension. Cross-level structural tension between K0 and K1 is defined by:
T0,1 = g(∆ − Θ0 , P1 − Θ1 ).
If T0,1 exceeds its dimensional threshold Θ1,dim , the emergent axis becomes unstable or collapses.

P.3.17 5. Conceptual examples
Emergence of the first axis from minimal differences. Any situation where a raw distinction (e.g.,
“state A differs from state B”) can be stabilised and parameterised corresponds to a realisation of the
K0→K1 transition. The axis A1 embodies this stabilised distinction.
Boundary formation. Once the axis exists, boundaries become meaningful:
∂Ω(K1 ) = {s ∈ Ω(K1 ) | ∇A1 reaches a threshold}.
First flows. With an axis and boundaries in place, gradient-like flows arise: an impossibility in K0 , but
a natural consequence of the stabilised distinction in K1 .
These examples illustrate the global significance of the K0→K1 transition:
It is the birth of all representable structure in the continuum hierarchy.
P.3.18 K1–K2 cross-level structure
The transition K1 → K2 marks the emergence of geometric and energetic structure from the minimal
representational continuum. Where K1 contains a single axis, primitive potentials and trivial flows, K2
introduces:
• multiple axes forming a coordinate structure,
• explicit potential–gradient relations,
• non-trivial flows J2 ,
• causal ordering,
• and a richer domain Ω(K2 ) supporting physical dynamics.
The cross-level structure captures how the simple representational geometry of K1 is extended into
the physical-like geometry of K2 .

P.3.24 K2–K3 cross-level structure
The transition K2 → K3 describes the emergence of the chemical continuum from a physical continuum

K3 is the first continuum supporting templating, catalysis, and information-like persistence via molecular states.

P.3.30 K3–K4 cross-level structure
The transition K3 → K4 marks the emergence of the biological continuum from the chemical continuum.

• metabolic cycles and buffering loops,

This is the birth of the first living-like continua: systems capable of maintaining non-equilibrium

The role of the K3 →K4 transition is the stabilisation of structure through controlled non-equilibrium

P.3.36 K4–K5 cross-level structure
The transition K4 → K5 marks the emergence of the neuronal continuum from the biological continuum.
While K4 supports gradients, membranes, and metabolic cycles, K5 introduces:
• electrical excitability and membrane voltage dynamics,
• ion channels with discrete open/closed states,
• propagating electrical events (proto-spikes),
• refractory mechanisms and excitability thresholds,
• spatial propagation along membranes and early network structure,
• attractor-like patterns forming proto-information flows.
This is the birth of nervous-system–like organisation: structure capable of encoding, propagating and
transforming electrical signals.

P.4 Cycle Structure in the Ontology of Continua
This master section provides the unified formal framework for cycle structure in the Ontology of Continua
(OC). Cycles constitute the central mechanism of structural persistence: a continuum remains alive if and
only if it maintains at least one structurally stable cycle that stays within its admissible state space Ω(K)
and maintains positive continuumness k(K, t). The material below consolidates all general results on
cycles across levels K0 –K12 , independent of domain-specific interpretations.
P.4.1 Definition of Cycles
A cycle of a continuum K is a closed trajectory
C : [0, τ ] → Ω(K),

C(0) = C(τ ),

such that:
1. C(t) remains strictly inside the admissible domain: dist(C(t), ∂Ω(K)) > 0;

2. the flow field J(t) supports the trajectory: Ċ(t) = J C(t), t ;
3. the cycle forms a stable attractor under the evolution operator E : K(t) → K(t + dt).
A cycle is structurally stable if perturbations of potentials, flows or thresholds do not destroy its
closed form: there exists ε > 0 such that all trajectories with initial distance < ε return to the cycle
within bounded time.

329

P.4.2 Role of Cycles in Continuum Persistence
In OC, cycles are not dynamical ornaments but structural necessities. They serve several essential functions:
• Maintain distance from the boundary ∂Ω(K). Without stable cycles, trajectories generically reach
the boundary, where thresholds saturate and the continuum collapses.
• Stabilise potentials and flows. Cycles maintain oscillatory, periodic, quasi-periodic or recurrent
regimes that preserve the structural viability of K.
• Carry the measure of continuumness. The contribution of cycles enters explicitly into the global
measure k(K, t) through their stability, diversity and distance to ∂Ω(K).
• Ensure structural identity. The presence of characteristic cycle complexes allows a continuum to
preserve its structural type across time.
As a consequence, the disappearance of all structurally stable cycles coincides with the death of the
continuum.
P.4.3 Cycle Complexes
For most continua, cycles do not appear in isolation but in interconnected clusters called cycle complexes.
A cycle complex Ccx is a finite or countably infinite collection of cycles {Ci } satisfying:
1. shared supporting flows;
2. structural compatibility under perturbations of thresholds;
3. existence of transition paths between cycles that do not reach ∂Ω(K).
The maximal cycle complex Cmax (K) is the set of all cycles that remain stable under the full threshold
landscape Θ(K).
Theorem 7 (OC Core) states that
Cmax (K) = ∅

⇐⇒

Ω(K) = ∅,

i.e. death is equivalent to the disappearance of the maximal cycle complex.

OC defines several universal metrics on cycles, needed for expressing continuumness, structural tension
and stability criteria.

P.4.5 Cycle Dynamics and Operator Q
The operator Q defines the time-evolution of cycle structure:

Core behaviours captured by Q include:
• Cycle formation: birth of new cycles when flows become recurrent and thresholds stabilise oscillations.
• Cycle stabilisation: increase of S(C) and reduction of oscillatory distance to the attractor.
• Cycle deformation: changes in length, shape or period due to modifications in potentials or flows.
• Cycle destruction: collapse when S(C) → 0 or flows fail to support recurrence.
This operator interacts with all other structural operators (F, G, H, R, S, U ) and contributes directly

P.4.6 Cycles Across the K-Hierarchy
Cycles appear at every level of the continuum hierarchy, though their interpretations differ:
• K1 : periodic field or geometric oscillations.
• K2 : coherence cycles, topological defects, phase loops.
• K3 : catalytic cycles in RAF networks.
• K4 : metabolic and membrane-maintenance cycles.
• K5 : excitation–repolarisation cycles (proto-spikes).
• K6 : cognitive feedback loops and prediction cycles.
• K7 : institutional cycles and cooperation loops.
• K8 : infrastructural and energy-logistics cycles.
• K9 , K10 : theoretical and meta-theoretical cycles.
Despite these differences, all such cycles share: closure inside Ω(K), positive distance to ∂Ω, and
stabilising interaction with thresholds.
P.4.7 Cycles and Dimensional Transitions
Dimensional birth (Kx → Kx+1 ) requires that cycles at level Kx approach the dimensional threshold
Θdim (Kx ) in such a way that their representational capacity becomes insuﬀicient. Loss of cycle stability
is one of the earliest indicators of an impending dimensional transition.
P.4.8 Summary
Cycles encode the persistence, identity and structural viability of continua across all domains. Their
stability, diversity and organisation form a key component of continuumness k(K, t). The disappearance
of all structurally stable cycles corresponds to the death of a continuum, while deformation and emergence
of new cycles signal structural reorganisation or dimensional transition.
331

P.4.9 Cycles on K0
Level K0 represents the meta-ontological background of the Ontology of Continua. It possesses no geometry, no time, no admissible state space in the sense of Ω(K), no flows J, no thresholds Θ, and no
operators of evolution. For this reason, the notion of a cycle cannot be defined on K0 .
P.4.10 Absence of State Space and Time
Cycles require:
1. a non-empty state space Ω(K);
2. a notion of time or parametrisation t ∈ [0, τ ];
3. a flow field J generating closed trajectories.
None of these structures exist on K0 . Formally:
Ω(K0 ) = ∅,

∂Ω(K0 ) undefined,

JK0 undefined,

and no parameter t exists that could index a trajectory.
Therefore, a cycle
C : [0, τ ] → Ω(K), C(0) = C(τ ),
cannot be formulated.
P.4.11 Structural Reason
Level K0 is not a continuum but a logical condition of possibility for continua of levels K1 and above.
It establishes no dynamical or geometric structure from which cycles could emerge. All cycle-related
notions—length, stability, distance to boundary, cycle complexes, or contributions to continuumness—
are strictly inapplicable.
P.4.12 Implication for Higher Levels
The absence of cycles on K0 implies:
• the concept of time τ (K) begins only at K1 , where a continuous axis is first defined;
• the first non-trivial cycles appear at K1 as trivial or degenerate oscillatory structures of a onedimensional field;
• structural cycles in the full sense (stability, distance to ∂Ω, interaction with thresholds) emerge only
at levels K2 and above;
• the birth of cycles is itself a signature of the phase transition K0 → K1 .
P.4.13 Summary
No cycles exist on K0 . Cycle structure becomes meaningful only beginning with K1 , where time, state
space and flows first appear. Accordingly, the file cycles_k0.tex records a formal non-existence
statement, required for the internal consistency of the cycle taxonomy across the entire hierarchy of continua.

P.4.18 Role of K1 Cycles in the Hierarchy

P.4.45 Cycles on K5
Level K5 corresponds to the early neural (bioelectrical) continuum. It is defined by the presence of
an excitable membrane, ion-channel architecture, threshold-governed spikes, recovery dynamics, and

the system with excitability, signalling, rhythmicity and proto-network coordination.

P.4.46 Overview of Cycle Structure on K5

P.5 Structural Jets
The jet formalism introduced in this section provides a unified, dimension-agnostic description of infinitesimal structural propagation across all continua in the Ontology of Continua (OC). While the operators E,
Ψ, Φ and U describe macroscopic evolution, embedding, deformation of admissible regions and global
continuumness, the jet hierarchy captures the local differential structure governing how continua deform
along their axes, potentials, flows, thresholds, and boundary gradients.
In classical mathematics, jets represent truncated Taylor expansions of smooth functions. In OC, jets
generalise this idea: a jet is a local, structurally admissible fragment of continuum evolution, encoding
all allowed derivatives of all structural components up to a specified order. This includes derivatives of:
• axes A(t) and their deformation modes,
• potentials P (t) and their gradients ∂P /∂A,
• thresholds Θ(t) and their rate of change,
• flows J(t), including cross-level flows and boundary exchange,
• cycles C(t) and their infinitesimal stability conditions,
• admissible regions Ω(K) and their boundary geometry ∂Ω(K),
• continuumness k(t) and its differential response.
Thus, a jet represents the infinitesimal content of the universal evolution operator:
E(K(t), M (t)) = K(t + ∆t),
providing a differential expansion that allows OC to connect macroscopic evolution to local geometric
constraints.

P.5.2 Role of Jets in Universal Dynamics
Jets serve four structural functions:
(1) Local generator of global evolution. While E provides the global update, jets describe its infinitesimal expansion:
E(K(t)) = K(t) + dt · J 1 (K) + dt2 · J 2 (K) + · · · .
(2) Compatibility conditions for Ψ and Φ. The embedding operator Ψ and the evolution of the ambient
space Φ must satisfy jet-consistency constraints, ensuring that:
J n (Kx ) ⊆ J n (Mx ).
(3) Local structure of phase transitions. Every dimensional transition (e.g., Kx → Kx+1 ) begins as
a jet instability: an nth-order divergence along a new axis.

• K9 : theoretical jets (paradigm deformation, model flux).
• K10 : meta-theoretical jets (functorial consistency).
• K11 : hyper-theoretical jets (modal universe curvature).
• K12 : universal jets (derivatives of structural laws).
All specialised jet files extend this master definition.

P.5.5 Summary
This master section establishes jets as the infinitesimal, level-agnostic formalism linking all structural
components of OC. It provides the foundation for each specialised jets-file that follows, ensuring consistency across K0 → K12 and integration with the universal operators E, Ψ, Φ, and U .
P.5.6 Jets on K0
The level K0 represents the degenerate, pre-geometric continuum of the Ontology of Continua (OC). It
contains no axes, no potentials, no thresholds beyond the minimal existence threshold Θ0 = ε > 0, and
no temporal evolution. Consequently, the jet structure on K0 is both trivial and foundational: it provides
the limiting case against which all higher-order jets are defined.
Formally, the structural content of K0 is given by:
K0 = (S, ∆, C),
where S is an undifferentiated structural substrate, ∆ is the minimal distinction required for the existence of a continuum, and C denotes the admissible compositions of distinctions. No metric, topological,
temporal, or dynamical structure exists at this level.
Thus K0 admits only the zero jet, representing the fact that no derivatives of any structural quantity
can be defined.
P.5.7 Definition of Jets on K0
Since K0 possesses no time parameter, no axes, and no dynamical fields, the general definition of n-jets
collapses to the trivial object:
J n (K0 ) = {0}
for all n ≥ 0.
This means:
• no quantities can vary with time (time does not yet exist),
• no gradients can be defined (no axes exist),
• no flows can be defined (no admissible transitions),
• no thresholds evolve (only the existence threshold Θ0 ),
• ∂Ω(K0 ) is static and degenerate.
The jet formalism therefore records the essential fact that K0 exhibits zero differential structure. All
higher jet structures J n (Kx ) for x ≥ 1 must reduce to J n (K0 ) in the appropriate singular limit.
367

P.5.8 Jet Constraints and Admissibility
The existence of jets at K0 reduces to the requirement that the minimal threshold of existence is respected:
T0 < Θ0 = ε.
If this condition fails, the continuum does not exist at all:
K0 = ∅.
Since K0 has no time evolution, the inequality is structural rather than dynamical; it represents the
minimal consistency condition of the pre-continuum. Any attempt to introduce derivative-like behaviour
would violate admissibility, since no such behaviour is defined.

• the notion of time as the parameter of evolution.

P.5.11 Jets on K1

P.5.19 Jets on K2

gradients, and geometric contributions to the energy and tension. Jets on K2 therefore include both temporal and spatial components. They encode the fine-scale behaviour of fields near percolation thresholds,
cluster boundaries, and structural transitions that enable the emergence of higher-order continua such as
K3 .

P.5.66 Jets on K6
The continuum level K6 describes cognitive organisation: axes of representation, prediction, attention
and control, structured by potentials (prediction error, salience, valence), flows (selection, binding, modelupdates) and thresholds for coherence and stability. Jets on K6 capture infinitesimal variations of cognitive states and models along these axes and provide a differential view on how small perturbations in
inputs, internal parameters or structural constraints propagate through the cognitive continuum.
We denote the cognitive continuum by

K6 = Ω(K6 ), A6 , P6 , Θ6 , J6 , C6 , k6 (t) ,
where Ω(K6 ) is the space of admissible cognitive states, A6 the set of representational and control axes, P6

385

error, …), J6 the cognitive flows, C6 the cycles (attention, learning, consolidation, …), and k6 (t) the

Jets on K6 describe derivatives of these objects with respect to the underlying axes and parameters
and therefore encode how micro-perturbations in A6 , P6 or Θ6 deform Ω(K6 ) and the flows J6 .
P.5.67 State fields and cognitive coordinates
A cognitive state at time t can be written as a field
x : A6 → R n ,
assigning to each representational axis a ∈ A6 a finite vector of activations or parameters. In practice, A6
may contain axes for sensory features, abstract concepts, task variables, latent factors, or decision-relevant
dimensions.
We write x(a) for the local state along axis a and collect these values into a global state x ∈ Ω(K6 ).
A change of state under a small perturbation δa of an axis is described by the jet
j 1 x(a) ≃ x(a) + ∂a x(a) δa,
where ∂a x(a) is the derivative of x with respect to the axis a. Higher-order jets capture more complex
dependencies (e.g. curvature, mixed derivatives across axes).
P.5.68 Potentials and their jets
Central potentials on K6 include prediction error, salience, and value-like quantities. Let

denote prediction error, salience and value potentials, respectively. Given a cognitive state x and a model
m, we can write
Ppred = Ppred (x, m),

Psal = Psal (x, m),

Pval = Pval (x, m).

Jets of these potentials describe how small changes in state, model or axes change the underlying
cognitive pressures. For example, for a representational axis a ∈ A6 , the first jet of prediction error along
a is
j 1 Ppred (a) ≃ Ppred (x, m) + ∂a Ppred (x, m) δa.
Large values of ∂a Ppred identify axes along which the system is particularly sensitive to perturbations.

P.5.70 Jets at the interface with K5
The coupling between K5 (bioelectrical excitable continua) and K6 (cognitive continua) is mediated

where no extra brace appears in the derivative term. This jet captures how small changes in the excitability axis (e.g. effective channel density, gating kinetics, or patch composition) alter the local membrane
potential.
On the K6 side, an axis of proto-representation Arep may be driven by spike statistics (rates, synchrony,
patterns). A jet of a representational coordinate xrep with respect to a spiking feature s can be written as
j 1 xrep (s) ≃ xrep (s) + ∂s xrep (s) δs.
Non-zero ∂s xrep indicates an effective projection from spike-space to representational space and thus
supports the emergence of cognitive axes from underlying electrical dynamics.
P.5.71 Jets of thresholds and boundary deformations
Thresholds on K6 (e.g. prediction-error threshold Θpred , complexity threshold Θcomp , coherence thresholds) define the boundary ∂Ω(K6 ) of admissible cognitive states. Jets of thresholds describe how boundary conditions deform under structural or parametric changes.
For a threshold Θi ∈ Θ6 depending on a parameter λ we have
j 1 Θi (λ) ≃ Θi (λ) + ∂λ Θi (λ) δλ.
Similarly, jets of the boundary itself can be written in terms of normal variations along ∂Ω(K6 ), capturing
how regions of admissible cognition expand, contract or change shape under slow structural evolution.
P.5.72 Jets and the evolution of k6 (t)
The measure of cognitive continuum strength k6 (t) depends on the structure of Ω(K6 ), the richness and
stability of cycles C6 , and the balance of flows J6 . Jets of k6 (t) with respect to parameters or axes quantify
how small changes in structure influence overall cognitive viability.
For a parameter λ we write
j 1 k6 (t; λ) ≃ k6 (t; λ) + ∂λ k6 (t; λ) δλ.
If ∂λ k6 > 0 in some direction, then small perturbations along λ increase the strength of the cognitive
continuum; if ∂λ k6 < 0 they weaken it. Jets therefore provide a local, differential tool for mapping
directions of stabilisation, destabilisation and possible transition paths towards higher levels (e.g. K7 ) or
towards collapse of K6 .

P.6 Processes
Processes constitute the dynamic layer of the Ontology of Continua (OC). A process is defined as any
structured transformation
P : Ω(K) −→ Ω(K)
regulated by the internal axes A(K), potentials P (K), flows J(K), thresholds Θ(K), structural tension
T (K), and the operators Ψ, Φ, Λ, U , X.
A process exists only if the continuum K maintains non-zero continuumness:
k(K, t) > 0,
and the transformation remains within the admissible region:
P(s) ∈ Ω(K)

∀ s ∈ Ω(K).

This master module provides the unified framework for all process-descriptions in OC and applies to
every level K0 –K12 .
P.6.1 Definition of a Process
A process on a continuum K is a tuple:


Π(K) = Ω(K), A(K), P (K), J(K), Θ(K), C(K), T (K), k(K), O ,

where O = {Ψ, Φ, Λ, U, X} is the set of universal OC operators.
Formally, a process is a map:
P(t) : Ω(K, t) → Ω(K, t + ∆t)
satisfying:
409

1. Admissibility: P(t)(Ω(K, t)) ⊆ Ω(K, t + ∆t);
2. Threshold compliance: fΘ (s) ≤ 0 for all evolved states s;
3. Flow coherence: J(K, t) must permit the transition enforced by P;
4. Cycle compatibility: P either preserves or transforms the existing cycles C(K) without destroying
the structural coherence of K;
5. Continuity condition: k(K, t + ∆t) ≥ 0, and death is defined by k → 0.
P.6.2 Operators and Processes
Processes arise through the universal operators:
• Ψ: generative operator (birth of distinctions, axes, and new states);
• Φ: structural operator (reconfiguration, alignment, mapping);
• Λ: boundary operator (modifies ∂Ω, creates new regions);
• U : evolution operator (global update of k, T , J, P , Θ);
• X: collapse operator (extinction, fragmentation, death).
Every process is expressible as a composition of these:
P = Λα ◦ Φβ ◦ Ψγ ◦ U δ ◦ Xϵ ,
with exponents indicating activation or multiplicity.
P.6.3 Classes of Processes
We classify processes into six universal families:
1. Generative processes (Ψ-dominated): birth of axes, dimensions, states, or entire continua.
2. Structural processes (Φ-dominated): rearrangement of A, P , J, or internal geometry of Ω(K).
3. Boundary processes (Λ-dominated): modifications of ∂Ω(K), creation or destruction of admissible regions.
4. Evolutionary processes (U -dominated): updates of tension, thresholds, flows, and continuumness.
5. Cyclic processes (C(K)-dominated): self-sustaining loops generating stability and coherence.
6. Collapse processes (X-dominated): destruction, degeneration, fragmentation, or death of the continuum.
Every specific continuum K exhibits its own instantiation of these universal classes.
P.6.4 Conditions for the Existence of Processes
For a process to exist at time t:
k(K, t) > 0,
T (K, t) < Θdeath ,

410

Ω(K, t) 6= ∅,
and
J(K, t) supports the transformation.
Violating any of these conditions induces a collapse trajectory under X.
P.6.5 Birth of a Process
A process is born when:
• new distinctions emerge (via Ψ),
• A(K) gains a new axis,
• P (K) changes beyond a generative threshold Θgen ,
• a new region of Ω(K) becomes accessible,
• a cycle C(K) begins to self-close,
• structural tension T crosses a metastable boundary.
Birth is always accompanied by a local increase in k(K).
P.6.6 Evolution of a Process
A process evolves according to:


A(t), P (t), Θ(t), J(t), T (t), k(t).
The evolution is coherent if:
C(K, t) 6= ∅

and

P.6.7 Death of a Process
A process dies when any of the following occur:
k(K, t) → 0,
T (K, t) > Θdeath ,
∂Ω(K) undergoes fragmentation,
Jsupport < Jcritical ,
C(K, t) breaks (cycle collapse).
Death may be localized (partial collapse) or global (K itself collapses).

P.6.9 Processes Across Levels K0 –K12
The nature of processes varies with level:
• K0 : pre-continuum proto-processes (formation of distinctions).
• K1 : geometric and energetic processes.
• K2 : dynamical and temporal processes.
• K3 : chemical reactions, bond formation/breaking.
• K4 : metabolic, osmotic, excitability processes.
• K5 : network, signaling, proto-cognitive processes.
• K6 : cognitive, representational, inferential processes.
• K7 : social, normative, institutional processes.
• K8 : civilizational, infrastructural, systemic processes.
• K9 : theoretical processes (model formation).
• K10 : formal, logical, recursive processes.
• K11 : cross-model, intertheoretic processes.
• K12 : meta-dynamic processes among model-spaces.
At each level, processes inherit the universal schema but operate on different structures of Ω(K) and
∂Ω(K).
P.6.10 Processes and M-Spaces
In M-spaces, processes are governed by:
ΘM , AM , ∂Ω(M ), J M , C M ,

A process in an M-space may induce:
• birth of new continua,
• branching of K-levels,
• dimensional shifts,
• cross-level fusions,
• global reconfiguration of Ω.
M-processes obey the same universal schema but take place in the superstructure where K0 –K12
reside as objects.
